title: Paying for Exclusion: When Access Is the Real Asset
documentTitle: United States v. Live Nation Entertainment & Ticketmaster — Exhibit PX0813 (Redacted)
emailSubject: Re: AEG at Hollywood Bowl - Ben Platt - April 2022
excerptForBlog:
Brian Smith (Live Nation): AEG has the Ben Platt tour. AEG are asking to come into the venue during our time frame. I want to say we don't work with AEG here as this will then allow them to include The Bowl when they are making a pitch to a potential client. On the other hand, this is a sold out show during a traditionally slow time frame at the Bowl. LAPA described AEG as a content provider NOT a co-promoter. It feels like it could be a can of worms for us to even buy this show.

Andy Hewitt: The bowl has been off limits to AEG during our season. We have paid a premium for the bowl to keep AEG from having access within our season. It seems like LAPA has come up with a way to have a huge guarantee from us and allow AEG in their time period. I think we should discuss in our negotiations with them.

Colin Lewis (Live Nation): All good, completely agree with you, no AEG under any circumstances.

sourceCase: United States v. Live Nation Entertainment, Inc. & Ticketmaster L.L.C.
lessonTitle: Paying for Exclusion: When Access Is the Real Asset
situation: In a March 2021 email thread, three Live Nation executives discuss whether to allow AEG — a direct competitor — to bring a Ben Platt tour into a venue during Live Nation's contracted season. The core tension: the show is sold out during a slow period, which is commercially attractive, but letting AEG in would give them a foothold — and a reference point — they currently lack.
insight: Andy Hewitt makes the hidden logic explicit: Live Nation 'paid a premium for the bowl to keep AEG from having access within our season.' The venue deal isn't just about booking shows. It's a **exclusivity-as-moat** play. By controlling access to a key venue, Live Nation denies a rival a credential they could use in future pitches to artists and promoters. One sold-out show isn't the risk — the risk is that AEG gets to say 'we play the Bowl too.' Brian Smith spots this first, noting that LAPA framed AEG as a 'content provider NOT a co-promoter,' which looks like a semantic workaround designed to blur the exclusivity boundary. Colin Lewis closes the thread with a hard line: 'no AEG under any circumstances.' The decision isn't about this show. It's about not letting a short-term revenue gain erode a long-term competitive barrier.
application: Map the assets in your business that serve double duty — they generate revenue AND block a competitor from building a reference or capability. Before accepting any revenue from a rival (a partnership, a white-label deal, a shared platform), ask: does this give them something they couldn't otherwise claim? If yes, price the exclusivity or walk away. That boundary is often worth more than the deal.
pullQuote: The most valuable thing you can own isn't the venue — it's the right to keep your competitor out of it.
leadershipTraits: spots strategic risk inside routine decisions
values long-term position over short-term revenue
closes ambiguity fast with a clear line
